newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia Yield Spreads-Underperfrom despite data.
newsitem.headline: Australia Yield Spreads-Underperfrom despite data.

text.p: Australian bonds underperformed despite local inflation in the second quarter being well below that of its dollar bloc partners.

The strong local price action, and yield spread contraction to the bloc, running into the data left the market vulnerable to profit-taking when the inflation outcome came in only just below market expectations, traders said.

Headline inflation in the second quarter fell 0.2 percent for an annual rate of just 0.3 percent, while the policy sensitive underlying rate rose 0.3 percent for 1.7 percent annually, its lowest since the series started in 1971.
Analysts at Colonial State Bank pointed out Australia's 0.3 percent annual headline inflation compares with 1.5 percent in Canada, 1.1 percent in N.Z. and 2.2 percent in the U.S.

The 10-year bond yield dropped to its lowest level in 3-1/2 years to around 6.40 percent on the data, but quickly retraced some of the move with an expected 50 basis point cut in official interest rates fully priced in.

Some analysts believe that the market is now in the final stages of its rally since April, which has taken the 10-year yield down some 175 basis points, and that if the Reserve Bank does ease policy, then it would be the last in the cycle.

"On a relative basis, I find it very hard to think that we could go much beyond the 30-35 basis point spread over the U.S. that we are at at the moment. If anything we could well go back out to 50 or 75," said Stephen Koukoulas, Citibank Australia chief economist.

The market had gone into the data extremely bullish, not only on the expected outcome of the data, but also on the back of a strong rally in U.S. Treasuries following comments by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan.
In his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony, Greenspan said that U.S. growth was slowing for the time being, heading off the need for now to raise interest rates.
He was also confident that U.S. inflation would be modest in 1997.
The U.S. Treasury market rallied strongly in New York on Greenspan, which saw the price of the U.S. 30-year bond jump over 1-1/2 points, and the advance continued in Tokyo.

"The real risk in the short-term is that U.S. bond yields continue to fall. So rather than seeing further spread contraction to the U.S. market, its (the local market) is going to keep up with the U.S.," said Shane Oliver, chief economist at AMP Society.
